idiom_name: nested key class guarded by the authorised class's private static #brand (runtime-enforced; JavaScript has no compile-time access control)
implementation_notes: JavaScript has no compile-time access control and constructors cannot be private; what it has is hard runtime privacy - #-prefixed elements cannot be referenced outside the class that declares them, and a violation is a syntax error (MDN). The faithful shape is therefore a nested key class whose constructor compares its argument with the authorised class's private static #brand: only that class body can produce the brand, so only it can mint keys, and a forged key throws a TypeError at run time. When the grantee is a module, scope can replace the brand: keep the key class unexported and hand keys out from the module's own functions. Because the enforcement is runtime, treat the token as a capability check rather than the compile-time grant the pattern describes, and never as a security boundary against code running in the same realm.
pitfalls: The brand is only as private as the realm: code holding the class object can call the key constructor and gets a runtime TypeError - a check, not a compiler proof.
Re-exporting or bundling the key class (or its module) widens the grant silently; module scope only holds while the binding stays unexported.
A debugger or a patched class can replace the brand, and dynamic code cannot reach # elements only because the syntax forbids it.
